Key Research Thinking Patterns: Fully Digital Phased Array Architecture Integration: Transitioning from analog dish-based systems to all-digital S-band polarimetric phased arrays to enable rapid volume scanning and high-resolution vertical sampling, validated through the development and operational assessment of the Horus radar system.

Advanced Pattern Synthesis and Beamforming Optimization: Employing non-linear optimization frameworks, such as Bézier-surface parametrization and genetic algorithms, to synthesize custom multi-peak and spoiled transmit beams that enhance sidelobe isolation and two-way pattern performance while managing power density trade-offs.

Self-Calibration and Mutual Coupling Mitigation: Developing reference-based mutual coupling calibration techniques using far-field measurements and UAS validation to ensure polarimetric accuracy and enable autonomous startup calibration for large-scale digital arrays, achieving pattern agreement within ±0.15 dB.

Non-Linear Signal Processing for Reduced Aperture Systems: Designing and testing staggered pulse-repetition time (PRF) sequences and iterative signal processing algorithms to maintain aircraft tracking and weather surveillance capabilities on reduced-aperture configurations (50-100%) for small platform deployment.
Summary Description: Mark Yeary is a principal investigator specializing in the development of next-generation fully digital phased array weather radars, primarily through the Horus radar system at the University of Oklahoma. His research bridges atmospheric science and radar systems engineering, focusing on replacing legacy WSR-88D networks with high-temporal resolution, polarimetric digital arrays. Key methodologies include advanced digital beamforming, Bézier-surface pattern synthesis, and self-calibration techniques to mitigate mutual coupling. Yeary’s work addresses critical challenges in severe weather monitoring, quantitative precipitation estimation, and air surveillance, with a specific focus on enabling radar capabilities on reduced-aperture platforms for small-scale deployment. His contributions have significantly advanced the state-of-the-art in radar meteorology and electromagnetic signal processing, providing robust frameworks for high-accuracy, real-time atmospheric observations.
